subject: Q re covariates and sex chromosome

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Q re covariates and sex chromosome
parts:
I received the following email and thought it and my response may be of broader interest.

I’m working on a project to identify QTL in a hybrid cross between two plant species with heteromorphic sex chromosomes and sexual dimorphism.  Currently I’m using your R/qtl pakage to run my analysis but I have a couple of questions.
 
My study systems consist on a CP cross, with the presence of sex chromosomes and sexual dimorphism. I have 314 individuals and 655 SNP markers distributed in 12 linkage groups.
 
As a first approach I’m running single QTL scans with the interval mapping “em” to detect for plausible QTLs and then I’m running the multiple QTL model comparison to estimate the LOD and PVE values and the possible interaction between QTLs. However, because my plants are sexually dimorphic I have biological reasons to include sex as a covariate and also to test for for the interaction between this covariable and the QTLs. The question will be:  when is the best time to include the covariable interaction, on the first interval mapping scan or just in the model comparison? 
When I run the scan just with the cov=sex (after estimating the thresholds) I end up with more QTLs than when I include cov=sex plus intcov=sex.  I find less stringent the first approach and I can refine it with the model comparison, but I’m not sure what will be the difference. For some traits it makes a huge difference, between finding 2 QTLs with no interaction to  6 QTLs  with a lot of interactions. 
 
The second question will be how is the program dealing with defining a sex chromosome and using sex as a covariate compared to when you don’t have a define sex chromosome and adding sex as a covariate. Because our sex chromosomes are still recombining a lot we explore the two possibilities and the QTLs that where significant with no sex chromosomes and sex as covariate, are not significant anymore when you have both: define sex chromosome and sex as covariate, and we are not very sure why.


There's discussion of the treatment of covariates in chapter 7 of the R/qtl book (http://www.rqtl.org/book).


If I know there's a sex difference in the phenotype, I'll always include sex as an additive covariate.


Including sex as an interactive covariate can be useful if there are QTL with big sex differences in their effect. In there are no such QTL x sex interactions, it's better to keep it as a strictly additive covariate, as the use of the interactive covariate will hurt your power to detect QTL.


Regarding sex chromosomes, R/qtl only handles the mammalian situation, of an X and a Y chromosome, with no recombination in the heterogametic sex.


I've dealt with cases where there was a sex "locus"; it seemed best to just treat it as an autosome, but to be sure to include sex as an additive covariate.


karl
